title: Tale of the Sultan and His Sons and the Enchanting Bird (हिन्दी)

full_text:
In Khorasan ruled a benevolent Sultan who fell victim to a deep melancholia that no physician could heal. An ancient traveler told him:
'O King, in the enchanted valley of Mount Qaf perches the Bird of Dawn, whose song restores youth and drives away all sorrows of the soul.'

The Sultan had three sons. The two elder princes, proud and selfish, volunteered to fetch the bird, demanding chests of gold and royal escorts. They rode forth, but upon reaching the pleasure city of Rey, squandered their gold on revelry and forgot their ailing father.

The youngest prince, Prince Yusuf, loved his father sincerely. He took only a sturdy horse and a loaf of barley bread, setting out alone into the wilderness.

Along the mountain path, Yusuf found a starving desert fox trapped beneath a fallen boulder. With great effort, Yusuf freed the animal and shared his bread.
The grateful fox spoke with human speech:
'Prince Yusuf, thy gentle heart preserves life. I shall be thy guide to Mount Qaf. When thou reachest the enchanted garden, thou wilt find the Bird of Dawn sleeping in an ebony cage. Beside it hangs a cage of solid gold. Beware! Place the bird only in the plain ebony cage; do not touch the golden one, or the palace guards will awaken!'

Yusuf reached the fairy palace, found the bird, but seeing its magnificent iridescent feathers, thought: 'Such a divine bird deserves a golden cage!'
The moment his fingers touched the golden wires, magical bells rang out, awakening the palace guards, who captured him!

The King of the castle spared Yusuf on one condition: that he bring him the Golden Steed of Baghdad.
Again the fox assisted Yusuf, warning him not to use the jeweled bridle. Once more, Yusuf's human frailty tempted him to touch the bridle, leading to a second trial: to bring the radiant Princess Shirin of Oman.

With the fox's counsel, Yusuf won Princess Shirin's heart by his honesty, obtained the Golden Steed, and secured the Bird of Dawn in the humble ebony cage.

Returning toward Khorasan, Yusuf encountered his two elder brothers, now destitute beggars. Overjoyed to see them alive, Yusuf embraced them, clothed them, and shared his provisions.
Yet envy consumed the elder brothers. At a remote well, they cast Yusuf into the abyss, seized Princess Shirin, the steed, and the bird, and presented them to the Sultan, claiming they had conquered Mount Qaf!

However, the Bird of Dawn remained silent, the steed refused oats, and Princess Shirin wept day and night.

Meanwhile, the faithful fox lowered a rope of vines into the deep well, rescuing Prince Yusuf.
Yusuf returned to his father's court in a humble shepherd's tunic. The moment he crossed the threshold, the Golden Steed whinnied with delight, Princess Shirin's face shone with radiance, and the Bird of Dawn burst into a celestial melody that instantly restored the Sultan's vitality!

Princess Shirin revealed the elder brothers' treachery. The Sultan banished the plotters, crowned Prince Yusuf as his heir, and celebrated his marriage with forty days of feasts, showing that pure virtue outshines the darkest betrayals.
moral: True loyalty and filial love are proven through selfless bravery, overcoming jealousy and deceit. [HI]
